pension scheme in the tax year 2024/25 and had an unused annual allowance brought
forward of £9,000.

only open to employees of the company. The cost to Herb plc of providing this benefit
was £780.

Herb plc’s workplace nursery. The total cost to the company of providing this nursery
place was £7,200 (240 days at £30 per day).

of Dill.
6 Dill also received various other taxable benefits during 2025/26.
Dill’s total employment income for the tax years 2024/25 and 2025/26 was £361,990,
inclusive of the items in Notes 1 to 6 above.

Self-employment
For the tax year 2024/25, Dill’s self-employed business did not make any profit and for the
tax year 2025/26, made a tax adjusted trading loss of £58,000. Dill will claim relief for this
loss against her total income for the tax year 2024/25.
Other income
1 On 1 November 2024, Dill received a premium bond prize of £1,000.

certificates from NS&I (National Savings and Investments).

2025/26?

 True False
The carry forward of trading losses is indefinite if the business
continues to trade.

When carrying forward trading losses, obtaining relief in a later
period is advantageous from a cashflow and time value of
money perspective.

Trading loss relief against total income permits the taxpayer to
relieve trading losses against the total income of the tax year
of the loss, and/or previous tax year.

title: JASON
text:
JASON  Walk in the footsteps of a top tutor
This scenario relates to three requirements.
You should assume that today’s date is 15 February 2025.
Jason is currently employed by Initial plc as a sales manager, but he is considering resigning
on 14 March 2025 and taking up an offer of employment with Subsequent plc which would
start on 15 March 2025. If employed by Subsequent plc, Jason will receive a higher base salary
and more benefits compared to if he remains employed by Initial plc. However, Jason wants
to know how much more income tax he will have to pay for the tax year 2025/26 should he
take up the new offer of employment. The following information is available for the tax year
2025/26:
Initial plc
1 If Jason remains employed by Initial plc, rather than taking up the offer of employment
with Subsequent plc, he will be paid a gross annual salary of £180,000 during the tax
year 2025/26.
2 Jason will contribute a total of £8,000 into Initial plc’s occupational pension scheme.
3 In addition to his salary, Jason expects to be paid the following bonuses by Initial plc:
Amount Date of payment Date of entitlement In respect of the year ended
£22,000 30 April 2025 15 March 2025 31 January 2025
£24,000 30 April 2026 15 March 2026 31 January 2026
4 Throughout the tax year 2025/26, Jason will be provided with free meals in Initial plc’s
staff canteen. The total cost of these meals to the company will be £1,440. Free meals
in the staff canteen are available to all of Initial plc’s employees.
Subsequent plc
1 If Jason takes up the offer of employment wi th Subsequent plc, then he will be paid a
gross annual salary of £205,000 during the tax year 2025/26.
2 Subsequent plc will contribute a total of £9,000 into the company’s occupational
pension scheme on Jason’s behalf.
3 Throughout the tax year 2025/26, Jason will be provided with a hybrid-electric car,
which has a list price of £62,500 and an official CO
2 emission rate of 25 grams per
kilometre.  It has an electric range of 25 miles. Jason will not be provided with any fuel
for private journeys.
4 For the period 6 April to 31 July 2025, Subsequent plc will provide Jason with living
accommodation in a property purchased by the company in 2014 for £140,000. The
property will be valued at £285,000 on 6 April 2025. Improvements costing £17,000
were made to the property during August 2023. The annual value of the property is
£4,800.

5 On 1 August 2025, Subsequent plc will prov ide Jason with an interest-free loan of
£140,000 to help him purchase a main residence. No loan repayments will be made
before 5 April 2026.
Where possible, Subsequent plc will payroll the taxable benefits provided to Jason so that
the related income tax liability will be collected under PAYE along with the tax on his salary.
Jason will not have any other income for the tax year 2025/26.
Required:
(a)  State one advantage and one disadvantage for an employee if their employer
payrolls the taxable benefits provided to the employee.
 (2 marks)
(b)  Calculate how much more income tax Jason will have to pay for the tax year 2025/26
if he takes up the offer of employment with Subsequent plc rather than remaining
employed by Initial plc. 
Notes:
1 Your answer should be based on separate calculations of Jason’s employment
income for the tax year 2025/26 under each employment alternative.
2 You should indicate by the use of zero (0) any items which are not taxable or
deductible.
3 You are not required to calculate Jason’s national insurance contributions
(NICs). (11 marks)
(c)  If Jason decides to resign as an employee of Initial plc on 14 March 2025, briefly
explain the main content and purpose of PAYE form P45.
 (2 marks)
 (Total: 15 marks)

This scenario relates to three requirements.

Employment

2 emission rate of 70 grams per kilometre. The car does not meet the real
driving emissions 2 (RDE2) standard. Poppy was not provided with any fuel for private
use.
3 Throughout the tax year 2025/26, Zune plc provided Poppy with two mobile
telephones. The telephones had each cost £480 when purchased by the company in
March 2025.
4 All of the taxable benefits provided by Zune plc to Poppy are payrolled.

Partnership
1 Poppy has been in partnership with Rose and Teasel since 6 April 2016, but Teasel
resigned as a partner on 6 July 2025. The partners have always shared profits equally.
2 For the year ended 5 April 2026, the partnership had a tax adjusted trading loss of
£19,500. This figure is before taking account of capital allowances.
3 The only item of plant and machinery owned by the partnership is a car with a CO 2
emission rate of 90 grams per kilometre. The car was used by Poppy and 70% of the
mileage was for private journeys. The written down value of the car as at 6 April 2025
was £8,400. The car was sold on 31 July 2025 for £5,400 and was not replaced.
UK Government securities (gilts)

accrued interest).

not make the balancing payment of £2,600 until 31 August 2026. She was not required to

benefits will have been reported to HM Revenue & Customs (HMRC). (2 marks)

Customs (HMRC) as a consequence of her not making the balancing payment for the
tax year 2024/25 until 31 August 2026. (3 marks)

title: KAZUO
text:
KAZUO
This scenario relates to five requirements.
You should assume that today’s date is 25 March 2025 and the tax rates and allowances
for the tax year 2025/26 apply throughout.
Kazuo is currently employed at a gross annual salary of £200,000. Kazuo will continue to earn
the same salary until he retires on 5 April 2029, at which point his income will reduce to gross
annual pension income of £55,000. This means that Kazuo is currently an additional rate
taxpayer, but will only be a higher rate taxpayer from when he retires on 5 April 2029.
Kazuo will undertake £40,000 of work on a freelance basis during the year ended 5 April 2026.
To carry out this work, Kazuo will form a new limited company, Zaoku Ltd, of which he will
be an employee. This freelance work will not involve any expenditure and will last for just
one year, from 6 April 2025 to 5 April 2026. Zaoku Ltd will prepare accounts for the year
ended 5 April 2026.

Kazuo is looking at three alternative ways of extracting the profits of Zaoku Ltd:
Alternative 1
After allowing for corporation tax, Kazuo will withdraw the entire net of tax profits as
dividends during the tax year 2025/26.
Alternative 2
Zaoku Ltd will pay Kazuo gross directors' remuneration of £8,000 and Zaoku Ltd will make a
pension contribution of £32,000 into a company occupational pension scheme on Kazuo's
behalf during the tax year 2025/26. Kazuo ha s sufficient unused pension annual allowances
so that a pension contribution of this amount will not result in an annual allowance charge.
Alternative 3
Kazuo will not withdraw any amounts during the tax year 2025/26. Instead, the net of tax
profits will be left undrawn in Zaoku Ltd until the tax year 2029/30 when Kazuo has retired.
He will then withdraw the entire net of tax amount as dividends in the tax year 2029/30.
Kazuo does not have any other income.
Required:
Assuming that Kazuo withdraws the entire net of tax profits of Zaoku Ltd as dividends
(alternative 1) during the tax year 2025/26:
(a) (i)  Calculate the corporation tax liability of Zaoku Ltd for the year ended 5 April
2026; and  (1 mark)
(ii)  Calculate the income tax payable by Kazuo in respect of his dividend income. 
 (2 marks)
Assuming that Zaoku Ltd will pay Kazuo gross directors' remuneration of £8,000 and Zaoku
Ltd will make a pension contribution of £32,000 into a company occupational pension
scheme on Kazuo's behalf (alternative 2) during the tax year 2025/26:
(b) (i)  Explain the corporation tax, income tax and national insurance contributions
(NICs) implications of alternative 2; and
  (3 marks)
(ii)  Calculate the tax saving of alternative 2 compared with alternative 1 (entirely
as dividends).  (1 mark)
Notes:
1 You are not expected to explain the tax implications of ultimately receiving a
pension from the pension scheme.
2 Zaoku Ltd is not entitled to the NICs annual employment allowance.
(c)  Calculate the tax saving in respect of Kazuo's dividend income and Zaoku Ltd's
corporation tax liability if Kazuo withdraws the entire net of tax profits of Zaoku Ltd
as dividends during the tax year 2029/30 (alternative 3) when Kazuo has retired,
rather than during the tax year 2025/26 (alternative 1).
 (3 marks)
 (Total: 10 marks)

(2)  On 1 August 2025, Luqe Ltd provided Sheldon with an interest-free loan of £80,000 (not

2026. The taxable benefit in respect of the loan is calculated using the average method.
(3)  Throughout the tax year 2025/26, Sheldon had the use of Luqe Ltd’s company gym.
The company gym is only open to employees of Luqe Ltd and the annual cost per
employee to the company of providing this benefit is £670.
(4)  Throughout the tax year 2025/26, Luqe Ltd provided Sheldon with living
accommodation. The company purchased the property on 1 January 2024 for

towards the use of the property. Running costs totalling £850 for the tax year 2025/26
were paid by Luqe Ltd. The property was furnished by Luqe Ltd at a cost of £20,000
when Sheldon first moved into the property on 1 January 2025.
(5)  Luqe Ltd paid £890 for medical insuranc e for Sheldon. If Sheldon had arranged the

(6)  Sheldon incurred business expenditure of £600 during the tax year 2025/26 which was
reimbursed by Luqe Ltd in full.
(7)  For the tax year 2025/26, Luqe Ltd deducted income tax of £60,560 under PAYE from
Sheldon’s earnings.

(1)  Sheldon owns 12 residential properties which are let out. The total rent received
during the tax year 2025/26 was £140,000.
(2)  In addition, on 6 April 2025, Sheldon received a premium of £45,000 on the grant of a
five-year lease for a freehold shop.
(3)  Sheldon’s expenditure in relation to the property business was £35,800 for the tax year
2025/26. This figure includes:

replaced washing machines which had been bought for £600 each in 2018. The
new washing machines were similar to the ones replaced.
(c)  £1,600 for legal fees in relation to the grant of the five-year lease for the

title: KAGAN
text:
KAGAN
This scenario relates to four requirements.
You should assume that today’s date is 4 April 2025.
On 2 April 2025, Kagan inherited some quoted ordinary shares valued at £510,000 following
the death of his aunt. Kagan is unsure whether to retain the shares or sell some of them in
order to make some alternative investments.
Kagan is aged 61 and is an additional rate taxpayer. Prior to the inheritance, his taxable
income, consisting entirely of employment income, for the tax year 2025/26 would have
been £400,000. The income tax liability on this income for the tax year 2025/26 would have
been £166,203.
Prior to receiving the inheritance, Kagan’s chargeable estate for inheritance tax (IHT)
purposes was valued at £1,700,000. IHT of £550,000 would be payable were he to die in the
near future.
Retain the inherited shares
If Kagan simply retains the inherited shares, then he will receive dividend income of £15,300
during the tax year 2025/26. This is in addition to his employment income of £400,000.
Sell some inherited shares and make four alternative investments
Kagan is considering selling some of his inherited shares (for which there has only been a
minimal increase in value since he inherited them) to fund the following four investments, all
of which will be made at the start of the tax year 2025/26:
1 Kagan will make a gross personal pension co ntribution of £100,000. Kagan is a member
of a pension scheme, but has not made any contributions in recent years because his
income has been substantially lower than it is for the tax year 2025/26. He therefore
has sufficient unused annual allowances to cover a pension contribution of £100,000.
Kagan will immediately withdraw £25,000 of  the pension fund tax-free. This is the
permitted tax-free amount. However, no pension will be taken during the tax year
2025/26.
2 Kagan will invest £50,000 in premium bonds. The expected amount of premium bond
prizes which will be received during the tax year 2025/26 is £700.
3 Kagan will invest the maximum permitted amount of £20,000 in a cash individual
savings account (ISA). The ISA will pay interest of £400 during the tax year 2025/26.
4 Kagan will purchase a freehold property for £295,000 (including all costs of purchase).
The property will be let out unfurnished, wi th Kagan receiving property income of
£9,600 during the tax year 2025/26.
After making these four investments, Kagan will be left with £65,000 of inherited shares, on
which he will receive dividend income of £450 during the tax year 2025/26. He will also have
his employment income of £400,000.
Kagan will not make any other disposals during the tax year 2025/26.

Required:
(a)  Calculate Kagan’s revised income tax liability for the tax year 2025/26 if he retains
the inherited shares.  (1 mark)
(b) (i)  Explain why little or no capital gains tax (CGT) will be payable if Kagan sells
some of his inherited shares.  (1 mark)
(ii)  Calculate Kagan’s revised income tax liability for the tax year 2025/26 if he sells
some of his inherited shares and makes the four alternative investments. 
Notes:
1  For this part of the question, you are expected to produce a full income tax
computation.
2 You should indicate by the use of zero (0) any items which are not taxable.
 (6 marks)
(c)  For each of the four alternative investments (pension contribution, premium bonds,
ISA and freehold property) state whether the investment will reduce Kagan’s
potential IHT liability compared to him retaining the inherited shares.

Note: For this part of the question, no computations are required. (2 marks)
  (Total: 10 marks)

title: TONIE (ADAPTED)
text:
TONIE (ADAPTED)
This scenario relates to three requirements.
Up to and including the tax year 2023/24, Tonie was resident in the UK for tax purposes,
spending more than 300 days in the UK each year. Tonie understands that for the tax year
2025/26, she will again automatically be treated as resident in the UK, but is unsure of her
residence status for the tax year 2024/25. For this tax year, Tonie was neither automatically
resident in the UK nor automatically not resident. Throughout the tax year 2024/25, Tonie
was travelling around the world and did not stay in any one country for longer than 30 days,
although she did spend a total of 50 days in the UK. Tonie has a house in the UK, but it was
let out throughout the tax year 2024/25. She is single, has no children, and stayed with a
friend on the 50 days that she spent in the UK. Tonie did not do any substantive work in the
UK during the tax year 2024/25.
The following information is available for the tax year 2025/26:
Employment
On 6 April 2025, Tonie, who is a software de veloper, accepted a one-year contract to
maintain websites for Droid plc. Droid plc treated the contract as one of employment, with
the payments to Tonie being subject to PAYE. However, Tonie thought that, because she was
working from home, her employment status should instead have been one of self-
employment.

1 For the term of the contract, from 6 April 2025 to 5 April 2026, Tonie was paid a fixed
gross amount of £6,200 a month. During the term of the contract, Tonie was not
permitted to work for any other clients. She was required to do the work personally,
not being permitted to sub-contract the work to anyone else.
2 During the term of the contract, Tonie worked from home, but had to attend weekly
meetings at Droid plc’s offices to receiv e instructions regarding the work to be
performed during the following week. During the period 6 April 2025 to 5 April 2026,
Tonie used her private car for business visits to Droid plc’s clients. She drove 2,300
miles, for which Droid plc paid an allowance of 60 pence per mile.
3 During the term of the contract, Tonie leased computer equipment at a cost of £180 a
month. This was used 100% for business purposes.
Property income
1 Tonie owns a freehold house which is let out. The total amount of rent received during
the tax year 2025/26 was £10,080.
2 Tonie partly financed the purchase of the property with a repayment mortgage, paying
mortgage interest of £4,200 during the tax year 2025/26.
3 During May 2025, Tonie purchased a new washer-dryer for the property at a cost of
£640. This was a replacement for an old washing machine which was scrapped, with
nil proceeds. The cost of a similar washing machine would have been £380.
4 During November 2025, Tonie purchased a new dishwasher for the property at a cost
of £560. The property did not previously have a dishwasher.
5 The other expenditure on the property for the tax year 2025/26 amounted to £1,110,
and this is all allowable.
6 During the tax year 2025/26, Tonie rented out one furnished room of her main
residence. During the year, she received rent of £8,580 and incurred allowable
expenditure of £870 in respect of the room. Tonie always uses the most favourable
basis as regards the tax treatment of the furnished room.
Other income
1 On 1 July 2025, Tonie inherited £100,000 (nomin al value) of gilts paying interest at the
rate of 3%. The inheritance was valued at £120,000. Interest is paid half-yearly on
30 June and 31 December based on the nominal value. Tonie sold the gilts on
30 November 2025 for £121,250 (including accrued interest).
2 On 31 January 2026, Tonie received a premium bond prize of £100.
3 On 31 March 2026, Tonie received interest of £520 on the maturity of savings
certificates from NS&I (National Savings and Investments).
Required:
(a) Explain why Tonie was treated as not resident in the UK for the tax year 2024/25.

 (2 marks)
(b) List FOUR factors which are indicators of Tonie being treated as employed in relation
to her contract with Droid plc rather than as self-employed. 
 Note: You should confine your answer to the information given in the question.
 (2 marks)
(c) On the basis that Tonie is treated as employed in relation to her contract with Droid
plc, calculate her taxable income for the tax year 2025/26. 
 Note: You should indicate by the use of zero (0) any items which are not taxable or
deductible. (11 marks)
  (Total: 15 marks)

title: BERTIE
text:
BERTIE
This scenario relates to two requirements.
You should assume that today’s date is 25 March 2025.
Bertie is the managing director of, and 100% shareholder in, Rebite Ltd.
For the past few years, Bertie has taken a high level of director’s remuneration from Rebite
Ltd to fund his personal pension contributions and the lease payments on his private car.
However, Bertie has now realised that these are not the most tax beneficial arrangements,
and is therefore considering more beneficial alternative arrangements.
Existing arrangements

This scenario relates to two requirements.

She prepared her first accounts for the year to 5 April 2026.

which are intended to simplify tax accounting for small businesses.
In the year to 5 April 2026 she has the following transactions:
1 Ethel earned income of £74,500 during the year. At 5 April 2026 £10,000 of the income

running costs of the car for the year. She has used the car 40% of the time for private

that she elects to prepare her accounts using the accruals basis. 

This scenario relates to four requirements.
You should assume that today’s date is 15 December 2025.
Zhi has been self-employed since 2007, preparing accounts to 31 December. On
1 December 2025, Zhi purchased a new freehold warehouse for £164,000 for use in his
business, but this purchase has resulted in Zhi having cash flow problems. He has various tax
payments becoming due over the next two months, and would like to reduce or postpone
these payments as much as possible.
Income tax and national insurance contributions (NICs)
Zhi’s income tax liabilities and class 4 NICs for the tax years 2023/24 to 2025/26 (inclusive)
are, or are forecast to be:
 2023/24 2024/25 2025/26
 £ £ £
Income tax liability 25,200 27,600 18,000
Class 4 NICs 4,084 4,204 3,724
Zhi has not made any claims to reduce his payments on account.
Capital gains tax (CGT)
Zhi has a CGT liability of £17,520 becoming due for payment on 31 January 2026. This is in
respect of a freehold office building which wa s sold for £210,000 on 10 December 2024,
resulting in a chargeable gain of £76,000. The office building had always been used for
business purposes by Zhi.
Zhi is a higher rate taxpayer. No claim has been made for rollover relief.

Value added tax (VAT)
Zhi has forecast that he will have to pay VAT of £20,200 on 7 February 2026 to HM Revenue
& Customs (HMRC) in respect of the VAT quarter ended 31 December 2025.
On 12 December 2025, Zhi dispatched goods relating to an exceptionally large credit sale of
standard-rated goods of £45,600 (inclusive of VAT). He has not yet issued a sales invoice for
this sale.
Because the customer is unlikely to pay until 28 February 2026, Zhi is considering not
issuing a sales invoice until 1 February 2026.
PAYE and NICs
Zhi will have to pay PAYE and NICs of £5,526 electronically on 22 January 2026 to HMRC in
respect of his two employees for the tax month running from 6 December 2025 to 5 January
2026.
This includes amounts for bonuses, which Zhi was planning to pay to his two employees on
1 January 2026, but he could delay payment until 10 January 2026. The bonuses are in
respect of the year ended 31 December 2025, and they will be treated as being received on
whichever is the date of payment.
The first employee has a gross annual salary of £20,000 and is to be paid a bonus of £1,500.
The second employee has a gross annual salary of £55,000 and is to be paid a bonus of
£5,000.
Required:
(a) Calculate the amount by which Zhi can claim to reduce his self-assessment income
tax and NICs due for payment on 31 January 2026 without incurring interest or
penalties.
  (2 marks)
(b) Calculate the amount by which Zhi’s CGT liability due for payment on 31 January
2026 will be reduced if he makes a claim for rollover relief based on the warehouse
purchased on 1 December 2025 for £164,000.  Assume that tax rates and allowances
for the tax year 2025/26 apply throughout.
  (3 marks)
(c) Explain whether Zhi can reduce the amount of VAT payable on 7 February 2026 by
not issuing a sales invoice for the credit sale of £45,600 until 1 February 2026, and, if
so, by how much the payment will be reduced.  (2 marks)
(d) Calculate the amount by which Zhi’s PAYE and NICs due on 22 January 2026 will be
reduced if he delays the payment of employee bonuses until 10 January 2026, and
state when the postponed amount will be payable. 
Note: Your calculations should be based on annual income tax and NIC thresholds.
 (3 marks)
 (Total: 10 marks)

JADE (ADAPTED)
This scenario relates to three requirements.
You should assume that today’s date is 15 December 2025.
Jade is self-employed and is normally subject to income tax at the higher rate of 40%.
However, because of some exceptionally large on e-off contracts, Jade has forecast that her
trading profit for the year ended 5 April 2026 will exceed £200,000, meaning she will pay
income tax at the additional rate of 45% for the tax year 2025/26.
Jade is going to undertake four measures ai med at reducing her income tax liability and
national insurance contributions (NICs) for the tax year 2025/26:
Employment of daughter
Jade’s daughter, Emerald, has recently retu rned to the United Ki ngdom after travelling
overseas. She currently has no income for the tax year 2025/26. For the three-month period
ended 5 April 2026, Emerald will be employed by Jade’s business at a gross monthly salary of
£2,000, payable on the 5th of the month. This salary is reasonable in relation to the duties
that will be performed by Emerald.
Capital expenditure
Jade was planning to purchase new office equi pment for £14,000 on 10 April 2026, but this
expenditure will instead be brought forward to 1 April 2026. This will be her only capital
expenditure in the tax year 2025/26.
Bonus
Jade has one key employee who was largely re sponsible for obtaining the large contracts.
This employee, who has a gross annual salary of £65,000, will be paid a bonus of £10,000 on
1 April 2026.
Drawings
Jade was planning to take £100,000 out of the business as drawings during the tax year
2025/26, but will instead take reduced drawings of £80,000.
Required:
(a) Briefly explain the difference between tax evasion and tax avoidance.  (2 marks)
(b) Calculate the income tax payable and class 1 NICs suffered by Emerald for the tax
year 2025/26. (2 marks)
(c) Calculate Jade's overall saving of income tax and class 4 NICs for the tax year 2025/26
if she undertakes the four tax planning measures.
Note: You should show by how much each of the four measures will reduce Jade's trading
profit and the resulting tax and class 4 NIC saving for Jade. (6 marks)
 (Total: 10 marks)

 £

text:
JACK (ADAPTED) Walk in the footsteps of a top tutor
This scenario relates to four requirements.
You should assume that today’s date is 15 March 2026 and that the tax rates and
allowances for the tax year 2025/26 continue to apply.
Jack, aged 44, is a widower following the recent death of his wife. He has just cashed in a
substantial share portfolio and is now considering what to do with the proceeds.
Gift to a trust
The value of Jack’s estate is in excess of £1,000,000, and he is worried about the amount of
inheritance tax which will be payable should he die. His wife’s nil rate band was fully used
when she died.
Jack is therefore planning to make an immediate lifetime cash gift of £300,000 to a trust with
the funds then being held for the benefit of his two children aged 10 and 12. Jack has not
made any previous lifetime gifts.
Personal pension contribution
The only pension contributions which Jack has made previously are a gross amount of £1,000
per month which he saves into a personal pension scheme. Jack has continued to make these
contributions throughout the tax year 2025/26. Although Jack has been saving into this
scheme for the previous 15 years, he is concerned that he is not saving enough for his
retirement. Jack therefore wants to make the maximum possible amount of additional gross
personal pension contribution for the tax year 2025/26, but only to the extent that the
contribution will attract tax relief at the higher rate of income tax.
Jack is self-employed. His trading profit is £112,000 for the tax year 2025/26 and the previous
five tax years. He does not have any other income and expects to make the same level of
profit in future years.

Individual savings account (ISA)
Jack has never invested any amounts in ISAs. During the next 30 days he would like to invest
the maximum possible amounts into stocks and shares ISAs.
Required:
(a) Explain, with supporting calculations where necessary, why it is good inheritance tax
planning for Jack to make the immediate lifetime cash gift of £300,000 to a trust. 
Note: You are not expected to consider taper relief. (3 marks)
(b) (i)  Advise Jack of the amount of additional gross personal pension contribution
he can make for the tax year 2025/26 which will benefit from tax relief at the
higher rate of income tax, and explain why this is a tax efficient approach to
pension saving.
  (4 marks)
(ii)  Calculate the amount of unused pension annual allowances which Jack will be
able to carry forward to the tax year 2026/27 if the contribution in (i) above is
made.  (1 mark)
(c) Advise Jack as to the maximum possible amount which he can invest into stocks and
shares ISAs during the next 30 days.  (2 marks)
  (Total: 10 marks)
SELF-ASSESSMENT

text:
ERNEST VADER (ADAPTED) Walk in the footsteps of a top tutor
This scenario relates to four requirements.
You should assume that today’s date is 30 June 2027.
You are a trainee Chartered Certified Accountant and are dealing with the tax affairs of Ernest
Vader.
Ernest’s self-assessment tax return for the tax year 2025/26 was submitted to HM Revenue
& Customs (HMRC) on 15 May 2026, and Ernest paid the resulting income tax liability by the
due date of 31 January 2027. However, you ha ve just discovered that during the tax year
2025/26 Ernest disposed of some shares, the details of which were omitted from his self-
assessment tax return. The capital gains tax liability in respect of this disposal is £18,000, and
this amount has not been paid.
Ernest has suggested that since HMRC’s right to initiate a compliance check into his self-
assessment tax return for the tax year 2025/26 expired on 15 May 2027, no disclosure should
be made to HMRC of the capital gain.
Required:
(a) Briefly explain the difference between tax evasion and tax avoidance, as well as the
general anti-abuse rule and how HMRC would view the situation if Ernest Vader does
not disclose his capital gain.
  (4 marks)
(b) Briefly explain from an ethical viewpoint how you, as a trainee Chartered Certified
Accountant, should deal with the suggestion from Ernest Vader that no disclosure is
made to HMRC of his capital gain.  (3 marks)

(c) Explain the penalties which your firm, as tax agents, could be liable to, if a compliance
check is commenced by HMRC and the firm fails to supply the information requested by
HMRC.  (2 marks)
(d) State the period for which late payment interest will run assuming that HMRC
discover the capital gain and raise an assessment on 15 July 2027 in respect of Ernest
Vader’s capital gains tax liability of £18,000 for the tax year 2025/26, and that this
amount is then paid on 31 July 2027.  (1 mark)
(Total: 10 marks)

title: FOGO LTD AND NETTA LTD
text:
FOGO LTD AND NETTA LTD
Fogo Ltd has one 100% subsidiary, Netta Ltd.
Fogo Ltd
During the year ended 30 September 2025, Fogo Ltd made the following capital disposals:
On 31 October 2024, Fogo Ltd sold an investment property which had been let out to tenants
since it was acquired. The investment property was sold to an unconnected company for
£625,000. It had cost £500,000 when it was acquired in February 2011.
On 4 May 2025, Fogo Ltd sold a freehold warehouse which it had used exclusively in its trade.
The warehouse was sold to an unconnected company for £560,000. It had cost Fogo Ltd
£100,000 when it was acquired in September 2001.
£

On 19 September 2025, Fogo Ltd sold a 4% shareholding in an unconnected trading company,
resulting in a capital loss of £25,000.
Indexation factors:
September 2001 to December 2018 0.593
February 2011 to December 2018 0.269
Netta Ltd
For the year ended 30 September 2025, Netta Ltd has a draft tax adjusted trading profit of
£180,000.
This figure has been calculated correctly but does not include interest payable or receivable.
Interest payable
On 1 October 2024, Netta Ltd borrowed £1,000,000 from a bank at an annual interest rate of
5%. During the year ended 30 September 2025, the interest payable of £50,000 was in
respect of the following:
1 Interest on £550,000 of the loan to acquire fixed plant and machinery for use in its
factory. The fixed plant and machinery has an expected useful life of 15 years.
2 Interest on £450,000 of the loan to acqui re a 3% shareholding in a trading company
called Jona Ltd.
Interest receivable
Netta Ltd’s financial statements for the year ended 30 September 2025 showed interest
receivable from investments of £35,000, of which £25,000 was received during the year and
£10,000 was accrued on 30 September 2025. There was no accrual brought forward at
1 October 2024.
1 What is the chargeable gain or allowable loss on the disposal of the investment
property on 31 October 2024 by Fogo Ltd, for the year ended 30 September 2025?


2 What is the chargeable gain on the disposal of the warehouse on 4 May 2025 by
Fogo Ltd, for the year ended 30 September 2025?
A £435,000
B £460,000
C £375,700
D £400,700
3 Select which TWO of the following statements are requirements for Fogo Ltd and
Netta Ltd to claim group rollover relief.
A Netta Ltd’s asset acquisitions took place within one year before and four years
after the disposal, which is a qualifying condition for group rollover relief
B The freehold warehouse sold by Fogo Ltd on 4 May 2025 is a qualifying asset
and was used in Fogo Ltd’s trade
C The shares acquired by Netta Ltd in Jona Ltd are qualifying business assets for
rollover relief as it is a trading company
D Netta is a 75% subsidiary of Fogo Ltd
£

4 Assuming Fogo Ltd’s gain is rolled over into the purchase of fixed plant and
machinery by Netta Ltd, select which of the following events will NOT result in the
gain becoming chargeable.
A Netta Ltd selling the fixed plant and machinery
B Fogo Ltd selling the shareholding in Netta Ltd
C Netta Ltd ceasing to use the fixed plant and machinery in the trade
D Ten years since the purchase of the fixed plant and machinery
5 What is Netta Ltd’s total non-trade loan relationship income for the year ended
30 September 2025?

title: DAVID AND ANGELA BROOK (ADAPTED)
text:
DAVID AND ANGELA BROOK (ADAPTED) Walk in the footsteps of a top tutor
This scenario relates to one requirement.
David and Angela Brook are a married couple. They disposed of the following assets during
the tax year 2025/26:
Jointly owned property
On 30 September 2025 David and Angela sold a house for £381,900. The house had been
purchased on 1 October 2005 for £86,000.
David and Angela occupied the house as their main residence from the date of purchase until
31 March 2009. The house was then unoccupied between 1 April 2009 and 31 December
2012 due to Angela being required by her employer to work elsewhere in the United
Kingdom.
From 1 January 2013 until 31 December 2019 David and Angela again occupied the house as
their main residence. The house was then unoccupied until it was sold on 30 September
2025.
Throughout the period 1 October 2005 to 30 September 2025 David and Angela did not have
any other main residence.
David Brook
On 5 May 2025 David transferred his entire shareholding of 20,000 £1 ordinary shares in
Bend Ltd, an unquoted trading company, to Angela. On that date the shares were valued at
£64,000. David’s shareholding had been purchased on 21 June 2022 for £48,000.
Angela Brook
On 7 July 2025 Angela sold 15,000 of the 20,000 £1 ordinary shares in Bend Ltd that had been
transferred to her from David. The sale proceeds were £62,400.
Neither David nor Angela has ever worked for Bent Ltd.
£

On 15 October 2025 Angela disposed of a small business she had been running part time for
many years.  The only chargeable asset in the business was a warehouse and this resulted in
a gain of £3,700.
Angela has taxable income of £27,145 for the tax year 2025/26. David does not have any
taxable income.
Required:
Compute David and Angela’s respective total capital gains tax liabilities for the tax year
2025/26. Ignore any payments on account.  (10 marks)

title: BILL DING
text:
BILL DING Walk in the footsteps of a top tutor
This scenario relates to three requirements.
Bill Ding has run a construction company, High Rise Ltd since he purchased the entire
shareholding for £112,000 in 2005. He has worked for the company since purchase.
Bill has decided to retire and on 17 August 2025 Bill made a gift of his entire holding of High
Rise Ltd shares to his daughter, Belle, who also works for the company. The market value of
the shares on that date was £260,000.
On 17 August 2025 the market value of High Rise Ltd’s chargeable assets was £180,000, of
which £150,000 was in respect of chargeable business assets. Bill and his daughter have
elected to hold over the gain on this gift of a business asset.
Belle plans to sell the shares in High Rise Ltd on 31 March 2026, when they are expected to
be worth £262,000 in order to fund a new business venture.
Neither Bill nor Belle has made any previous di sposals chargeable to capital gains tax, and
both are higher rate taxpayers.
Required:
(a) Calculate the gains arising and capital gains tax liabilities for Bill and Belle on the gift
of High Rise Ltd shares to Belle and the subsequent sale by Belle.

Assume that Bill and Belle make a joint claim for gift holdover relief, and state the
due date for this claim.  (5 marks)
(b) Recalculate the gains arising and capital gains tax liabilities for Bill and Belle,
assuming a joint claim for gift holdover relief is not made.  (3 marks)
(c) Briefly conclude, including a calculation of the tax saving, on which route would be
preferable for Bill and Belle.  (2 marks)
(Total: 10 marks)

You should assume that today’s date is 1 March 2026.
(a) This scenario relates to one requirement.
Ginger has a holding of 10,000 £1 ordinary shares in Nutmeg Ltd, an unquoted trading
company, which she had purchased on 13 February 2015 for £2.39 per share. The
current value of the shares as agreed with HM Revenue & Customs is £6.40 per share,
but Ginger intends to sell some of the holding to her daughter at £4.00 per share during
March 2026. Ginger and her daughter will elect to hold over any gain as a gift of a
business asset.
For the tax year 2025/26, Ginger will not make any other disposals, and has therefore
not utilised her annual exempt amount.
Required:
Explain how many £1 ordinary shares in Nutmeg Ltd Ginger can sell to her daughter
for £4.00 per share during March 2026 without incurring any capital gains tax liability
for the tax year 2025/26.
 
Your answer should be supported by appropriate calculations. (4 marks)
(b) This scenario relates to one requirement.
Innocent and Nigel, a married couple, both have shareholdings in Cinnamon Ltd, an
unquoted trading company with a share capital of 100,000 £1 ordinary shares.
Innocent has been the managing director of Cinnamon Ltd since the company’s
incorporation on 1 July 2015, and she curre ntly holds 20,000 shares (with matching
voting rights) in the company. These shares were subscribed for on 1 July 2015 at their
par value. Nigel has never been an employee or a director of Cinnamon Ltd, and he
currently holds 3,000 shares (with matching voting rights) in the company. These
shares were purchased from an existing shareholder on 23 April 2020 for £40,200.
Either Innocent or Nigel will sell 2,000 of their shares in Cinnamon Ltd during March

fully utilise their annual exempt amounts, an d they will each have taxable income of
£80,000.
Required:
Calculate the capital gains tax saving if the disposal of 2,000 shares in Cinnamon Ltd
during March 2026 is made by Innocent rather than Nigel.
  (6 marks)

title: DALJEET
text:
DALJEET Walk in the footsteps of a top tutor
This scenario relates to two requirements.
Please assume today’s date is 5 April 2025.
Daljeet wishes to sell personal assets to generate funds to pay his daughter’s university fees
and he has selected two assets that he is willing to sell. He will sell one of the assets to a third
party on 31 December 2025 and will make his decision based on the asset that will generate
the highest amount of net proceeds.
The assets Daljeet has identified as potential disposals are as follows:
1,000 shares in ABC Ltd
Daljeet acquired 1,000 shares in ABC Ltd, a trading company, on 7 June 2020 for £60,000
when he became an employee of the company. On 7 June 2021 ABC Ltd underwent a rights
issue, offering shareholders the opportunity to purchase 2 shares for every 5 shares already
held for £50 per share. Daljeet purchased the maximum number of shares.
ABC Ltd has 20,000 shares in issue.
If Daljeet sells the ABC Ltd shares, he will sell 1,000 shares worth £100,600 on 31 December
2025.
Holiday cottage
The cottage is currently worth £110,000 and legal fees in respect of the disposal are expected
to be £1,000. Repairs costing £3,500 were made to the cottage roof in December 2023
following damage caused by a storm.
Daljeet originally bought the cottage in May 2015 at a cost of £64,700. It has always been let
out and Daljeet has never occupied the property as his private residence.
Other information
Daljeet will be a higher rate taxpayer and will make no other disposals in the tax year
2025/26.
Required:
(a) Calculate which of the above asset disposals will result in the highest amount of
proceeds, after deducting tax and any costs of sale.

You should assume that Daljeet will claim any relevant reliefs where possible and
has not previously claimed any capital gains tax reliefs. (8 marks)
(b) Briefly explain why the disposal of either the ABC Ltd shares or the holiday cottage
will not be subject to inheritance tax.  (2 marks)
(Total: 10 marks)

text:
LUNA LTD Walk in the footsteps of a top tutor
This scenario relates to two requirements.
Luna Ltd had the following transactions in shares during the year ended 31 March 2026:
1 On 29 November 2025, Luna Ltd sold its entire shareholding of £1 ordinary shares in
Pluto plc for £53,400. Luna Ltd had originally purchased 16,000 shares in Pluto plc on
14 June 2011 for £36,800. On 22 May 2013, Luna Ltd sold 10,000 of the shares for
£46,200. Assume the indexation factors are as follows:
June 2011 to May 2013 0.063
May 2013 to December 2017 0.112
2 On 12 February 2026, Luna Ltd’s shareholding in Asteroid plc was taken over by
Comet plc. Luna Ltd had originally purchased 10,000 £1 ordinary shares in Asteroid plc,
and their indexed cost on 12 February 2026 was £33,000. Under the terms of the
takeover, for each of its £1 ordinary shares in Asteroid plc, Luna Ltd received £6.50 in
cash plus one £1 ordinary share in Comet plc. Immediately after the takeover, Comet
plc’s £1 ordinary shares were quoted at £4.50.
Required:
(a) Explain how the indexation allowance can be used when a company makes a capital
loss, or where the indexation allowance is greater than a company’s unindexed
gain.
  (2 marks)
(b) Calculate the chargeable gain arising from each of Luna Ltd’s transactions in shares
during the year ended 31 March 2026. When calculating the chargeable gain arising
from the disposal of the shareholding in Pluto plc, you should show full workings for
the share pool.
  (8 marks)
(Total: 10 marks)

Lebna’s chargeable estate
Lebna has a chargeable estate valued at £980,000. His estate includes a main residence
valued at £340,000 on which there is an outstanding interest-only mortgage of £152,000.
Under the terms of his will, Lebna has left his entire estate to his son.
Gift to son on 22 February 2021
On 22 February 2021, Lebna made a gift of 60,000 £1 ordinary shares in Blean Ltd, an
unquoted investment company, to his son. Before the transfer, Lebna owned all of
Blean Ltd’s share capital of 100,000 ordinary shares. The market value of Blean Ltd’s ordinary

Holding Market value per share
  40% £4.20
  60% £6.30

The gifts of £85 and £190 were to the same friend.

title: JESSICA
text:
JESSICA
This scenario relates to three requirements.
Jessica is an additional rate taxpayer and on 6 April 2025, she made a lifetime gift consisting
of both shares and cash to a trust, with the funds then being held for the benefit of her two
grandchildren aged three and four. Jessica unders tands that she will have to consider both
inheritance tax (IHT) and capital gains tax in re spect of these gifts, but the trust will pay the
IHT arising.
Jessica's gifts to the trust
Shares
100,000 £1 ordinary shares in Valuable Ltd, an unquoted non-trading (investment) company.
Jessica currently owns 150,000 shares out of Va luable Ltd’s issued share capital of 250,000
£1 ordinary shares. The current market value of Valuable Ltd’s ordinary shares is:
Holding Market value per share
20% £3
40% £4
60% £7
Jessica subscribed for her 150,000 shares in Valuable Ltd at their par value of £1 per share on
8 July 2007.
Jessica’s disposal of shares in Valuable Ltd will not qualify for business asset disposal relief or
investors’ relief or gift holdover relief for a gift of a business asset. Jessica will not make any
other disposals during the tax year 2025/26.
Cash
Cash totalling £250,000, of which £50,000 was held within cash individual savings accounts
(ISAs) and the remainder was in bank accounts earning interest.
Jessica has not made any previous lifetime gifts.
Jessica's income 2025/26
Jessica will be an additional rate taxpayer for the tax year 2025/26.
As a result of gifting the cash to the trust, Jessica will have no savings income for the tax year
2025/26. If Jessica had not made the gift, then she would have received savings income of
£6,250 on the cash held during the tax year 2025/26, of which £1,250 would have been from
ISAs.
As a result of making the gift of shares, Je ssica’s dividend income for the tax year 2025/26
was reduced from £24,000 to £8,000.
Required:
(a)  Calculate Jessica’s capital gains tax liability for the tax year 2025/26. (3 marks)
(b)  Calculate the lifetime inheritance tax (IHT) which will be payable as a result of Jessica
making both gifts to the trust.
Note: You should ignore the IHT annual exemption. (4 marks)
(c)  Calculate the reduction in Jessica’s income tax liability for the tax year 2025/26.
 (3 marks)

title: HARBOUR LTD (ADAPTED)
text:
HARBOUR LTD (ADAPTED)

Walk in the footsteps of a top tutor
This scenario relates to three requirements.
You should assume that today’s date is 25 March 2026.
Harbour Ltd has previously prepared accounts to 30 November, but has decided to change
its accounting reference date to 31 March to be coterminous with the corporation tax
financial year. The company’s forecast draft statement of profit or loss for the four-month
period ending 31 March 2026 is as follows:
 Note £
Operating profit 1 715,500
Other income:
Property business income 2 13,800
Chargeable gain 3 104,300
Interest expense:
Interest paid 4 (24,600)
Profit before income taxes  809,000
Notes
1 Depreciation of £11,760 and amortisation of leasehold property of £1,300 (see below)
have been deducted in arriving at the operating profit figure of £715,500.
 On 1 December 2025, Harbour Ltd acquired a leasehold office building, paying a
premium of £78,000 for the grant of a 20-year lease. The office building will be used
for business purposes by Harbour Ltd throughout the four-month period ending
31 March 2026.
2 Harbour Ltd lets out a freehold warehous e which is surplus to requirements. On
1 December 2025, the tenant paid rent of £15,600 for the six-month period to 31 May
2026. On 1 December 2025, Harbour Ltd paid insurance of £1,800 for the year ended
30 November 2026.
3 The chargeable gain is in re spect of the disposal of investments on 10 March 2026. No
indexation allowance is available.
4 The interest paid is in respect of Harbour Ltd’s 6% loan notes, with interest for six
months of £24,600 being paid on 1 January 2026. Interest of £12,300 will be accrued
at 31 March 2026, with the corresponding accrual at 1 December 2025 being £20,500.
The loan notes were issued in order to finance the company’s trading activities.
Capital allowances
The tax written down value of both the main pool and the special rate pool as at 1 December
2025 was £Nil.
On 12 January 2026, Harbour Ltd purchased plant and machinery for £548,000. This will be a
long-life asset for capital allowance purposes.

Required:
(a)  Calculate Harbour Ltd’s corporation tax liability for the four-month period ending
31 March 2026. 
 Note: Your computation should commence with the operating profit figure of
£715,500. (10 marks)
The directors of Harbour Ltd now realise that it will be beneficial for the company to prepare
accounts for the year ending 30 November 2026 rather than for the four-month period
ending 31 March 2026. This conclusion is based on the following information which is
available in respect of the period 1 April to 30 November 2026:
1 Harbour Ltd will not purchase any further plant and machinery during this period, so
the full annual investment allowance of £1,000,000 will be available in respect of the
long-life plant and machinery purchased on 12 January 2026 for £548,000.
2 Harbour Ltd will sell an investment on 10 Apr il 2026 and this disposal will result in an
allowable capital loss of £42,000.
Required:
(b) (i)  Briefly explain the difference between tax evasion and tax avoidance, and how
HM Revenue & Customs (HMRC) are likely to view the situation if Harbour Ltd
extends its accounting period in order to save corporation tax.
 (3 marks)
 (ii)  If Harbour Ltd prepares accounts for the year ending 30 November 2026 rather
than for the four-month period ending 31 March 2026, calculate the revised
figures that will be included in respect of capital allowances and chargeable
gains.
 (2 marks)
  (Total: 15 marks)

text:
DEIMOS LTD, ELARA LTD AND FENRIR LTD
This scenario relates to three requirements.
You should assume that today’s date is 5 March 2026.
You are a trainee Chartered Certified Accountant assisting your manager with the tax affairs
of three unrelated limited companies, Deimos Ltd, Elara Ltd and Fenrir Ltd.
Deimos Ltd
Deimos Ltd ceased trading on 30 September 2025, preparing its final financial statements for
the 17-month period 1 May 2024 to 30 September 2025. On 1 October 2025, the company’s
shareholders passed a resolution to commence winding up procedures. The winding up of
Deimos Ltd was completed on 28 February 2026, with the company ceasing to exist on that
date.
Elara Ltd
Elara Ltd’s summarised statement of profit or loss for the year ended 31 December 2025 is
as follows:
   Note £
Operating profit 1 612,900
Other income:
Loan interest receivable 2 1,100
Profit on disposal of freehold warehouse 3 99,300
Interest expense:
Interest payable 4     (900)
  –––––––
Profit before income taxes  712,400
  –––––––
Note 1 – Operating profit
Depreciation of £8,820, qualifying charitable donations of £2,300 and leasing costs of £4,200
have been deducted in arriving at the operating profit of £612,900. The leasing costs relate
to a car with an official CO
2 emissions rate of 124 grams per kilometre which was leased from
1 June 2025.
Elara Ltd incurred £2,576 on entertaining clients and £75 on gifts of calendars to customers
(each calendar costing £7.50 each and bearing the company's name). These costs have also
been deducted in arriving at the operating profit of £612,900.
Note 2 – Loan interest receivable
The loan was made for non-trading purposes on 1 October 2025. The loan interest of £1,100
was accrued at 31 December 2025.
Note 3 – Profit on disposal of freehold warehouse
On 21 December 2025, Elara Ltd sold a freehold warehouse for £204,000. The warehouse
had been purchased for £104,700 in 2016, and its indexed cost on 21 December 2025 was
£108,800. Structures and buildings allowances were not available on this warehouse.
Elara Ltd has made a claim to rollover the ga in on the warehouse against the replacement
cost of a new freehold warehouse which was purchased on 6 January 2026 for £168,000. The
freehold warehouse and the replacement warehouse have been, and are, used entirely for
business purposes by Elara Ltd.
Note 4 – Interest payable
The interest payable is in respect of Elara Ltd’s 4.5% loan notes which were repaid on
31 January 2025. Interest of £5,400 was paid on 31 January 2025, and an accrual of £4,500
had been provided for at 1 January 2025. The loan notes were issued in order for Elara Ltd to
purchase plant and machinery.
Capital allowances
The tax written down value of both the main pool and the special rate pool as at 1 January
2025 is nil.
On 10 February 2025, Elara Ltd purchased an overhead crane for £220,000. The crane is a
long-life asset.
On 1 March 2025, Elara Ltd purchased a new car with CO
2 emissions of 25 grams per
kilometre for £30,000.
Fenrir Ltd
Fenrir Ltd’s forecast corporation tax liability for the year ending 31 March 2026 is £132,500.
This is based on forecast taxable total profits of £530,000. Because these figures are relatively
high compared to previous years, Fenrir Ltd plans to take three measures prior to the end of
the company’s accounting period on 31 March 2026:
1  Four new cars will be purchased for a total cost of £64,000. All four cars will have zero
CO
2 emissions.
2  A dividend of £60,000 will be paid to the company’s shareholders.
3  Rent of £18,000 covering the six-month period 1 April to 30 September 2026 will be
paid in advance.
Required:
(a)  Identify Deimos Ltd’s accounting periods throughout the period 1 May 2024 to
28 February 2026.  (2 marks)
(b)  Calculate Elara Ltd’s taxable total profits for the year ended 31 December 2025. 
  Note: Your computation should commence with the operating profit figure of
£612,900, and should also list all of the items referred to in the scenario, indicating
by the use of zero (0) any items which do not require adjustment. (9 marks)
(c)  Calculate the amount of corporation tax which Fenrir Ltd will save for the year ending
31 March 2026 by taking the three measures prior to 31 March 2026.

 Note: Your answer should be supported by appropriate explanations. (4 marks)
  (Total: 15 marks)

LONG LTD AND ROAD LTD (ADAPTED) Walk in the footsteps of a top Tutor
(a) This scenario relates to one requirement.
 Long Ltd owns 100% of the ordinary share capital of Road Ltd. Long Ltd and Road Ltd
are both trading companies.
Long Ltd’s shareholding in Road Ltd was acquired on 15 January 2025 when that
company was incorporated. Long Ltd has prepared accounts for the year ended
31 March 2026, whilst Road Ltd has prepared accounts for the period 1 January 2026
(when the company started trading) to 31 March 2026.
The following information is available:
Long Ltd
1 The operating profit for the year ended 31 March 2026 is £384,400. Depreciation
of £43,050, amortisation of £5,000 and leasing costs of £3,600 have been
deducted in arriving at this figure. The amortisation relates to a premium which
was paid on 1 August 2021 to acquire a leasehold office building on a 20-year
lease. The amount of premium taxed on the landlord as income was £68,200.
 The office building was used for business purposes by Long Ltd throughout the
year ended 31 March 2026. The leasing costs relate to a car with a CO
2 emission
rate of 82 grams per kilometre, which was leased from 1 April 2025.

2 On 1 April 2025, the tax written down value of the plant and machinery main
pool was £44,800. On 10 June 2025, Long Ltd purchased a new lorry for £47,840
and a new car for £15,700. The car has a CO
2 emission rate of 42 grams per
kilometre. The car is used by the managing director of Long Ltd, and 40% of the
mileage is for private journeys.
3 On 1 February 2026, Long Ltd disposed of a 2% shareholding in an unconnected
company. The disposal resulted in a capital loss of £21,300.
Road Ltd
1 The operating loss for the three-month period ended 31 March 2026 is £26,100.
Donations of £2,800 have been deducted in arriving at this figure. The donations
consist of political donations of £400 and qualifying charitable donations of
£2,400.
2 On 3 October 2025, Road Ltd purchased a car for £11,600. The car has zero CO
2
emissions.
3 For the three-month period ended 31 Ma rch 2026, loan interest receivable was
£4,300. The loan was made for non-trading purposes.
4 On 18 March 2026, Road Ltd disposed of a 1% shareholding in an unrelated
company. The disposal result ed in a chargeable gain of £29,800. This figure is
after taking account of indexation.
Other information
Road Ltd is not expected to be profitable for the foreseeable future, and Long Ltd and
Road Ltd claim maximum possible group relief where group relief is available.
Required:
On the assumption that any available reliefs are claimed as soon as possible,
calculate the corporation tax liability of Long Ltd for the year ended 31 March 2026,
and of Road Ltd for the three-month period ended 31 March 2026.  (12 marks)
(b) This scenario relates to one requirement.
 Road Ltd’s recently appointed bookkeeper understands that the company must report
PAYE information to HM Revenue & Customs in real time. However, the bookkeeper
does not know how PAYE real time reporting works in practice, having previously only
produced payroll manually.
Road Ltd pays its employees at the end of each calendar month, with some employees
receiving taxable benefits. Road Ltd has chosen not to tax the benefits through the
payroll system.
Required:
Explain how and when Road Ltd will have to report real time PAYE information to
HM Revenue & Customs, and state what forms, if any, will have to be provided to
employees or submitted to HM Revenue & Customs following the end of the tax
year.
  (3 marks)
 (Total: 15 marks)

title: MAXIMUM LTD
text:
MAXIMUM LTD
This scenario relates to two requirements.
The following information is available in respect of Maximum Ltd for the year ended
31 March 2026:
Trading profit
The trading profit based on the draft accounts for the year ended 31 March 2026 is £127,200.
This figure is before making any adjustments required for:
(1)  A premium which was paid on 1 August 20 25 to acquire a leasehold office building on
an eight-year lease. The amount of premium assessed on the landlord as income was
£22,320. The office building was used for business purposes by Maximum Ltd
throughout the period 1 August 2025 to 31 March 2026.
(2)  Leasing costs of £10,300 which have been deducted in arriving at the profit of
£127,200. The leasing costs relate to two cars which have been leased since 1 April
2025. The first car has CO
2 emissions of 40 grams per kilometre and is leased at an
annual cost of £6,400. The second car has CO 2 emissions of 120 grams per kilometre
and is leased at an annual cost of £3,900.
(3)  Employee bonuses of £36,000, which have not been deducted in arriving at the profit
of £127,200, all of which relate to the year ended 31 March 2026. Maximum Ltd paid
£20,000 of the bonuses on 30 November 2026, with the remainder of £16,000 paid on
15 February 2027. No entitlement to the bonuses arose until the time that they were
paid.
Property business income
Maximum Ltd lets out a freehold warehouse which is surplus to requirements. The building
was let from 1 April to 31 October 2025 but, although it was available for letting, it was empty
from 1 November 2025 to 31 January 2026. Because it was not possible to find new tenants,
the warehouse was sold on 31 January 2026 (see chargeable gains).
The following income and expenditure was incurred during the period 1 April 2025 to
31 January 2026:
Date received/(paid)   £
1 January 2025 Rent for the six months ended 30 June 2025 8,400
1 April 2025 Insurance for the year ended 31 March 2026 (1,320)
1 July 2025 Rent for the four months ended 31 October 2025 5,600
31 October 2025 Repaid security deposit of one month’s rent (1,400)
20 January 2026 Advertising for tenants (720)
31 January 2026 Insurance refund (less an administrative fee) 190
Chargeable gains
Maximum Ltd made two disposals during the year ended 31 March 2026:
(1)  On 31 January 2026, Maximum Ltd disposed of a freehold warehouse (see property
business income) for £187,000. The disposal resulted in a chargeable gain of £43,300.
The warehouse was never used by Maximum Ltd for business purposes.
(2)  On 20 February 2026, Maximum Ltd disposed of a freehold factory for £142,000. The
disposal resulted in a chargeable gain of  £29,100. The factory was used by Maximum
Ltd for business purposes.
On 10 December 2025, Maximum Ltd had purchased a new factory for £342,000. This factory
is used for business purposes. Maximum Ltd made the maximum possible rollover relief claim
against the new factory cost of £342,000.
No rollover relief claim has been, or will be, made in respect of the premium paid for the
eight-year lease (trading profit note (1)).
Donations
During the year ended 31 March 2026, Maximum Ltd made qualifying charitable donations
of £2,800 and political donations of £700. Neither of these amounts have been deducted in
arriving at the trading profit figure of £127,200.
Subsidiary companies
Maximum Ltd has two subsidiary companies, bo th of which commenced trading on 1 April
2023. Each company made a trading profit for the year ended 31 March 2026. The following
information is available:
Subsidiary Percentage shareholding Trading profit
Xim Ltd 85% £21,400
Mum Ltd 65% £13,800
Neither company has any other income or outgoings, with neither making a trading profit for
the year ended 31 March 2025.
Brought forward losses
Maximum Ltd has the following brought forward amounts of unused losses from the year
ended 31 March 2025:
  £
Trading loss (288,200)
Property business loss (3,800)
Capital loss (4,900)
Required:
(a)  Before taking account of brought forward losses, apart from any losses which are
automatically relieved, calculate Maximum Ltd’s taxable total profits for the year
ended 31 March 2026. 
Note: Your computation should commence with the trading profit based on the draft
accounts figure of £127,200, indicating by the use of zero (0) any items that do not
require adjustment. (11 marks)
(b)  On the basis that the maximum possible loss relief and group relief claims are made
for the year ended 31 March 2026, calculate the total remaining amount of unused
losses which Maximum Ltd can carry forward to the year ended 31 March 2027.

Note: If possible, your loss relief claims should not result in donations becoming
unrelieved. (4 marks)
(Total: 15 marks)

 True False

customers paid within the 14-day period.

totalling £35,700 were received. This figure includes £690 for entertaining UK customers,
£1,200 for entertaining overseas customers, and £900 for mobile telephone calls (of which
20% related to private calls). All of these figures are inclusive of VAT.
Cessation
Mabel wishes to retire and is therefore going to cease trading on 31 March 2026. She will
deregister for VAT. Mabel is unsure whether she will sell the assets of her business separately
to different purchasers after ceasing to trade, or whether she will sell the entire business as
a going concern on 31 March 2026. During the previous three years, Mabel has purchased
the following non-current assets:
1 Computer equipment purchased during July 2023 for £4,100 and sold during
November 2025 for £350
2 A car purchased (for both business and pr ivate use) during August 2025 for £9,600
which Mabel still owns
3 Office equipment purchased during March 2026 for £7,400 which Mabel still owns.

1  What is the amount of output value added tax (VAT) payable by Mabel in respect of
her sales for the quarter ended 28 February 2026?
A  £18,424
B  £17,640
C £15,353
D  £19,600

of her purchases and expenses for the quarter ended 28 February 2026?
A  £5,920
B  £5,835
C £5,805
D  £5,605

A  Notification: 30 April 2026
 Deregistration 30 April 2026

 Deregistration 31 March 2026
C Notification: 31 March 2026
 Deregistration 31 March 2026
D  Notification: 31 March 2026
 Deregistration 30 April 2026

purchasers, how much output value added tax (VAT) will she have to pay on her final
VAT return, in respect of the non-current assets purchased during the three years
prior to the cessation of trading?
A  £3,400
B  £2,300
C £2,230
D  £1,480
5  What is the advantage for Mabel if she sells her entire business as a going concern
for value added tax (VAT) purposes?
A  No output VAT will be payable in respect of the sale of the business
B  The new owner must take over Mabel's VAT registration

title: ZIA
text:
ZIA Walk in the footsteps of a top tutor
This scenario relates to three requirements.
Zia has been registered for value added tax (VAT) since 1 April 2015.
The following information is available for the year ended 31 March 2026:
1 Sales invoices totalling £126,000 were issued, of which £115,200 were in respect of
standard-rated sales and £10,800 were in re spect of zero-rated sales. None of Zia’s
customers are VAT registered.
2 On 31 March 2026, Zia wrote off two impairment losses which were in respect of
standard-rated sales.
The first impairment loss was for £780, and was in respect of a sales invoice which had
been due for payment on 15 August 2025.
The second impairment loss was for £660, and was in respect of a sales invoice which
had been due for payment on 15 September 2025.
3 Purchase invoices totalling £49,200 were re ceived, of which £43,200 were in respect
of standard-rated purchases and £6,000 were in respect of zero-rated purchases.
4 Rent of £1,200 is paid each month. During the year ended 31 March 2026, Zia made
13 rental payments because the invoice dated 1 April 2026 was paid early on 31 March
2026. This invoice was in respect of the rent for April 2026.
5 During the year ended 31 March 2026, Zia spent £2,600 on mobile telephone calls, of
which 40% related to private calls.
6 During the year ended 31 March 2026, Zia spent £1,560 on entertaining customers, of
which £240 was in respect of overseas customers.
All of the above figures are inclusive of VAT where applicable. The expenses referred to in
notes 4, 5 and 6 are all standard-rated.
Zia does not use either the cash accounting scheme or the flat rate scheme.
He has forecast that for the year ended 31 March 2027, his total sales will be the same as for
the year ended 31 March 2026.
Required:
(a) Calculate the amount of value added tax (VAT) payable by Zia for the year ended
31 March 2026.
 
You should indicate by the use of zero any items referred to in notes 1 to 6 where
there is no VAT impact. (6 marks)
(b) Explain why Zia will be permitted to use the VAT flat rate scheme from 1 April 2026,
and state the circumstances in which he will have to leave the scheme. 
 (2 marks)
